questions.q: Per this lesson, what does it mean when resistance shows up even after a good stakeholder map, communication plan, and training?
options: It always means the communication plan failed completely
It means the program should be cancelled immediately
It means training was skipped
It's a normal part of the adoption arc, not necessarily a sign that something went wrong upstream
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that some resistance is a normal part of the adoption process, not proof of an upstream failure.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the root causes of resistance this lesson identifies?
options: Loss of informal control over a decision they used to make themselves
A full moon occurring during the rollout
Extra work with no visible benefit to the person
A genuine gap in how the new process handles their case
questions.explain: The lesson lists extra work with no visible benefit, past bad experience, genuine process gaps, and loss of informal control — not anything superstitious.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend doing when resistance traces back to a genuine process gap?
options: Ignore it since the rollout has already launched
Mandate compliance regardless of the gap
Immediately escalate the individual to the governance council
Route it back through the governance workflow as a real change request, not just manage it as a complaint
questions.explain: The lesson says a legitimate process gap should go through the governance workflow from Lesson 8 as a real fix, not just be managed as a complaint.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what's the risk of escalating resistance too early?
options: There is no risk to escalating early
It automatically triggers a policy rewrite
It burns trust and teaches people that raising concerns gets them labeled as a blocker
Early escalation always resolves the issue instantly
questions.explain: The lesson warns that escalating before genuinely trying to understand the resistance discourages people from raising legitimate concerns in the future.

questions.q: What judgment call does the lesson say escalation decisions ultimately come down to?
options: How many people are resisting, regardless of why
Whether the resistance was expressed in writing or verbally
Distinguishing "won't comply" from "can't yet comply," which only comes from actually listening first
Whether the person resisting has a senior job title
questions.explain: The lesson frames the key judgment call as distinguishing genuine refusal from an unresolved legitimate obstacle, which requires listening first.
